facts.statement: The genus Dsungaripterus was first described in 1964 by the paleontologist Yang Zhongjian.
facts.quote: Dsungaripterus was described in 1964 named by Yang Zhongjian.

facts.statement: Fossils of Dsungaripterus are found in the Wuerho Pterosaur Fauna group within the Junggar Basin of China.
facts.quote: Its fossils come from the Wuerho Pterosaur Fauna group (WPF) of the Tugulu Group, comprising sections of the Lianmuqin and Shengjinkou Formations of the Junggar Basin.

facts.statement: While some deposits containing Dsungaripterus fossils date to the middle Valanginian, the exact age range of these layers remains uncertain.
facts.quote: Both formations have been given various age estimates, with data suggesting at least some of the WPF date to the middle Valanginian, but the upper and lower bounds of these pterosaur bearing deposits remain unclear.

facts.statement: The species Dsungaripterus weii had a wingspan ranging from 3 to 3.5 meters.
facts.quote: Dsungaripterus weii had a wingspan of 3 - 3.5 m.

facts.statement: Dsungaripterus possessed a robust skeleton with thick bone walls, suggesting it spent most of its time on the ground.
facts.quote: Like most dsungaripteroids it had a rather robust skeleton with thick walls and stouty bodily proportions, suggesting a mostly terrestrial lifestyle.

facts.statement: The skull of Dsungaripterus measured over 46 cm in length and featured a low bone crest extending from the skull base to the middle of the beak.
facts.quote: The skull of Dsungaripterus, measuring over 46 cm long, bore a low bone crest that ran down from the base of the skull to halfway to the beak.

facts.statement: The front part of Dsungaripterus's jaws lacked teeth and was likely used to extract prey from rock cracks or sandy, muddy environments.
facts.quote: It had no teeth in the front part of its jaws, which were probably used to remove prey from cracks in rocks and/or the sandy, muddy inland environments it inhabited.

facts.statement: Dsungaripterus had flat, knobbly teeth at the back of its jaws adapted for crushing the shells of hard objects like shellfish.
facts.quote: It had knobbly flat teeth more to the back of the jaw that were well suited for crushing the armor of shellfish or other hard objects.

facts.statement: Researchers commonly interpret Dsungaripterus as a durophagous (shell-crushing) and possibly fish-eating pterosaur.
facts.quote: Thus, it is commonly interpreted that dsungaripterids were durophagous and possibly piscivorous pterosaurs.

facts.statement: Dsungaripterus had a wingspan measuring between 2 and 3 meters.
facts.quote: Medía entre 2 y 3 metros de envergadura.

facts.statement: Dsungaripterus was a large pterosaur with a head and neck size comparable to a human arm.
facts.quote: Era un pterosaurio de talla considerable, con la cabeza y el cuello del tamaño de un brazo humano.

facts.statement: Dsungaripterus had numerous rounded, blunt teeth, but its beak tip was toothless, pointed, and curved upward, likely used to probe sand and mud for worms and mollusks to crush with its posterior teeth.
facts.quote: Tenía numerosos dientes redondeados y romos, pero el extremo del pico carecía de ellos y era puntiagudo y curvado hacia arriba; posiblemente lo introducía en la arena y el lodo en busca de gusanos y moluscos a los que trituraría con sus dientes posteriores.

facts.statement: Yang classified Dsungaripterus as a member of the family Dsungaripteridae.
facts.quote: Dsungaripterus fue clasificado por Yang como un miembro de los Dsungaripteridae.

facts.statement: A 2019 study by Kellner and colleagues recovered Dsungaripterus outside the Azhdarchoidea, placing it within Tapejaroidea as a sister taxon to Noripterus.
facts.quote: In 2019, a different topology, this time by Kellner and colleagues, was published. In this study, Dsungaripterus was recovered outside the Azhdarchoidea, within the larger group Tapejaroidea, sister taxon to Noripterus.

facts.statement: The time range for Dsungaripterus is estimated from the Valanginian to the Barremian, between 137.05 and 121.4 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Valanginian to Barremian (137.05 to 121.4 million years ago)

rejected.statement: A 2014 phylogenetic analysis by Andres and colleagues placed Dsungaripterus within the clade Dsungaripteromorpha, specifically in the Dsungaripteridae as a sister taxon to Domeykodactylus.
rejected.quote: They recovered Dsungaripterus within the clade Dsungaripteromorpha (a subgroup within the Azhdarchoidea), more specifically within the Dsungaripteridae, sister taxon to Domeykodactylus.
